overview: This file traces American diplomatic and institutional efforts to monitor, interpret, and circulate Japanese print culture from 1940 through the wartime period. Its contents range from Embassy reporting on censorship—most notably the suppression of Gaiko Jiho and Tsuneo Yonaiyama’s pragmatic critique of Japan’s war in China—to diplomatic greetings, Japanese-Hungarian cultural relations, and Japan Institute publications promoting knowledge of Japanese government, society, culture, mobilization, and postal practices. It concludes with evidence of wartime magazine consolidation and a FORTUNE reprint intended to brief U.S. officials on Japan’s economic and strategic vulnerabilities and on contemporary interpretations of Japanese religion, imperial loyalty, sacrifice, and national psychology.
interest: Shows how knowledge of Japan was produced and repurposed, including Yonaiyama's censored China-war debate article and Japan Institute outreach.
